title: Which life stands highest: the household or renunciation?
claim: The Book of Virtue awards the first place twice. Chapter 3 says the texts' settled view sets the renouncer's greatness above every other excellence (21) and that those who have discerned the two states and taken on அறம் here stand highest in the world (23), and chapters 27 and 35 divide humanity into those who do தவம் or renounce completely and 'the rest', who are caught in desire or in the net (266, 348). Chapter 5 answers in the same register: the householder who lives by virtue gains nothing by going to the outside way (46), stands first among all who strive (47), has more endurance than those who do penance (48), and his life is the thing the word அறம் names (49). Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read 46's புறத்தாறு as renunciation, so the collision between 46 and 342/348 is in the commentaries, not only in Pope; Parimelazhagar fits the two chapters together as a ladder (fame and heaven for householders in 50, release for full renouncers in 348), and reads 49's 'அஃதும் ... நன்று' as granting renunciation parity with the household.
limits: The conflict softens on some readings: Manakkudavar takes 47's முயல்வார் as those who strive for wealth, so 47 does not rank the householder above ascetics, and he reads the 'அஃதும்' of 49 as the household life itself (good if the wife is not blameworthy), not as renunciation. Kalaignar reads 23 as choosing good over bad in general. The thread does not claim the Kural contradicts itself knowingly; it claims each chapter speaks in superlatives for its own subject and leaves the ranking to the commentators.

title: Renunciation rests on those who have not renounced
claim: The Kural says the ascetic's state is sustained by people who keep what he gives up. Having nothing is the nature of the vow (344), yet those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing if the ploughmen fold their hands (1036), and 263 assumes that 'the others' hold possessions in order to provide for renouncers (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). On who ranks higher, the book splits by chapter: the chapters on the household and on giving grant the ascetic his own virtue of endurance and award more of it to the provider (48: நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து; 225: enduring hunger comes behind removing it), while 263, on both Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's reading, concludes that தவம் exceeds giving (Manakkudavar: தானத்தினும் தவம் மிகுதியுடைத்து).
limits: 263 is phrased as a question (மறந்தார்கொல்) and its ranking of தவம் over giving is the commentators' inference, not the verse's statement. 1036 is in the Book of Wealth and praises farmers; its point about ascetics is incidental. The thread claims a dependence the book notes, not a doctrine it argues.

title: Which wealth is the true wealth?
claim: Four chapters crown a different thing as the wealth among wealths or the excellent wealth: grace (241, அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), not wanting (363, விழுச்செல்வம்), learning (400, கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and hearing (411, செவிச்செல்வம் ... செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை), while 751 says nothing but wealth is wealth (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). Each verse argues against material wealth by a different defect: 241 by who can hold it (even the base have it), 400 by whether it can be lost (Parimelazhagar: heirs, thieves, the strong and kings cannot take learning), 411 on Parimelazhagar's reading by its impermanence and painful fruit, and 363 by having nothing above it in either world. The form is the same and the winners and the reasons differ, which suggests a rhetorical figure that each chapter fills for its own subject rather than a single ranking. 751 inverts the move: the fact that wealth is found among the base, which 241 counts against it, is exactly the power 751 counts in its favour.
limits: The verses do not rank the crowned wealths against one another; 400 and 411 sit in adjacent chapters and neither mentions the other. 751 is in the Book of Wealth and speaks of standing in the world, not of the goods the Book of Virtue values, so its absolute is in a different register. No commentator treats these as a contradiction.

title: Wealth gives everything, on conditions the chapter does not state
claim: Chapter 76 makes large claims for wealth: nothing else makes persons of no account into persons of account (751), grace itself is a child nursed by wealth (757), and those who have made bright wealth in full have virtue and pleasure together for the asking (760, ஒண்பொருள் ... ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). The conditions come from inside the same chapter and from later ones. 754 requires wealth that came by right means and without wrong, 755 tells one to let go wealth that does not come with grace and love, 1009 uses 760's own word ஒண்பொருள் for wealth amassed by setting love aside and ignoring virtue and says others will take it, and 1002 names nearly 751's thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as the miser's delusion when it leads to not giving. 973, on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's reading of the high and low seats as wealth and poverty, limits 751 further: wealth gets a person regarded without making them great. Read together, chapter 76's promises hold for wealth rightly earned and spent, and the book supplies that limit elsewhere rather than in the promising verses.
limits: Parimelazhagar reads chapter 76 as the king's revenue (754's தீது as tyranny, 755's grace and love as the one-sixth tax), so on his reading 751-760 and the private miser of 1002 and 1009 concern different agents. 757's dependence of grace on wealth is not withdrawn anywhere; 755 only conditions which wealth may nurse it. The thread does not claim the Kural disparages wealth.
